analysis.one_liner: Opens the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge coastal plain to oil and gas drilling.
analysis.headline: The bill to open the Arctic Refuge to oil leasing, with 50 cosponsors and two committee hearings, never received a House vote and died in committee when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have overturned the legal ban on oil and gas drilling in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge's 1.5-million-acre coastal plain, ordering the Interior Department to hold lease sales there. It declared drilling 'compatible' with the refuge's purposes by law, narrowed the required environmental review to a single leasing alternative with a 20-day comment window, and restricted legal challenges to the D.C. appeals court under a heavy burden of proof. It also conveyed land to two Alaska Native corporations and set up a small aid fund for nearby communities.
analysis.who_benefits: Oil and gas companies, which would gain access to federal leases on the refuge's coastal plain, with a first sale required within 22 months offering at least 200,000 acres of the most promising tracts [S3]. Alaska Native corporations — the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and Arctic Slope Regional Corporation — would receive conveyed surface and subsurface land titles and hiring and contracting preferences [S3]. Local North Slope governments would get a share of lease revenue through an impact aid fund, though it is capped at $10 million [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Oil companies and Alaska Native corporations

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the 1980 law prohibiting oil and gas production in the Arctic Refuge and orders the Interior Department to run a competitive leasing program on the roughly 1.55-million-acre coastal plain [S2][S3].
Requires the first lease sale within 22 months of enactment, offering at least 200,000 acres of tracts with the greatest hydrocarbon potential [S3].

Conveys the surface estate of specified lands to the Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation and remaining subsurface estate to Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, clearing their Native land claims entitlements [S2][S3].

Creates a Coastal Plain Local Government Impact Aid Assistance Fund, financed by lease revenues, to help North Slope communities pay for firefighting, police, water, and medical services affected by drilling, capped at $10 million [S3].

Requires leases to carry a royalty of at least 12.5 percent, bans export of the oil produced, requires reclamation by lessees, and directs lessees to negotiate project labor agreements and use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public that owns the Arctic Refuge, which would lose its protection from industrial development permanently; the bill would strip the normal environmental review process (only one leasing alternative analyzed, 20-day comment window), narrow judicial review to the D.C. Circuit with a 'clear and convincing evidence' standard, and declare the Secretary's sole discretion over which lands stay closed [S3]. Congress also forgoes royalty and bonus revenue beyond the small capped impact fund, which comes from public lease receipts [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, via the Arctic Refuge itself

drawbacks.text: The bill deems leasing 'compatible' with the refuge's founding purposes by statute and declares the 1987 environmental statement sufficient, cutting off the normal review — it analyzes only one leasing alternative, accepts comments for just 20 days, and requires challenges to be filed in the D.C. Circuit with the Secretary's analysis presumed correct unless disproven by clear and convincing evidence [S3].
It makes this Act the Secretary's sole authority to close any coastal plain land to drilling, removing the ordinary flexibility to protect habitat as new information emerges [S2][S3].

The honest case for the bill: the coastal plain may hold significant domestic oil, the bill layers on real safeguards (winter-only exploration, seasonal calving closures, no surface occupancy in special areas, full reclamation liability), and the U.S. would collect royalties, bonuses, and jobs — supporters argued this served energy security.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was not a giveaway without conditions — it carried a 12.5 percent royalty floor, an oil export ban, reclamation liability, winter-limits, and project labor agreements. But it achieved drilling by legislative fiat: declaring the activity 'compatible' with a wildlife refuge, compressing environmental review to one alternative with a 20-day comment window, and funneling all legal challenges into a single court under a near-impossible standard of proof. The trade was permanent industrial development of the largest protected wild area in the country for uncertain oil quantities and a $10-million-capped local aid fund.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in the House Natural Resources Committee, which held two hearings but never voted to send it to the full House, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2005.

narrative.text: Rep. Don Young of Alaska introduced the bill on January 7, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Resources; the Interior Department was asked for its views [S1][S5].
The committee held hearings on the bill on March 12 and April 5, 2003 [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no markup, no committee vote, no floor vote — and the bill died at the end of the 108th Congress on January 3, 2005 [S1][S5].

Don Young reintroduced the same measure in each subsequent Congress; a nearly identical bill passed the House in 2005 as part of the energy debate, but the refuge remained closed to drilling through the end of 2005 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Arctic Refuge coastal plain stayed undeveloped, and the interests that wanted it that way — conservation groups, subsistence users, and the public that owns the refuge — were better off because the bill never reached a vote. Oil companies got no leases and no change in the law.

for.name: Rep. Don Young
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to open the Arctic Refuge coastal plain to oil leasing and pushed it through two committee hearings.

against.name: House Committee on Natural Resources
against.role: Committee of referral (chaired by Rep. Richard Pombo, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Held hearings on March 12 and April 5, 2003, but never reported the bill to the full House for a vote.

sides.party_line_note: The 50 cosponsors split 44 Republicans to 6 Democrats, so the push for refuge drilling ran overwhelmingly through the Republican side of the House, though a handful of Democrats joined.

industries.note: The bill hands the industry access to the Arctic Refuge coastal plain through mandatory lease sales, while shielding the process from full environmental review and from most judicial challenges. The industry's gain comes directly out of a publicly owned conservation area, and any effect on consumer fuel prices from Alaskan oil would be small and distant.

industries.industry: Alaska Native regional and village corporations (Arctic Slope Regional Corporation, Kaktovik Inupiat Corporation)
industries.note: The bill conveys long-sought land titles to these corporations and requires lessees to use best efforts to hire Alaska Natives and contract with Native corporations. Nearby communities would also get an impact aid fund capped at $10 million, though drilling on the refuge could affect the subsistence hunting those communities depend on.
